entities.name: Faustus of Riez
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Faustus of Riez was a prominent Bishop of Riez (Rhegium) in Southern Gaul (Provence), a leading opponent of Pelagianism. He played a crucial role in shaping the theological debates of his time, particularly with regards to the nature of original sin and the role of human free will.

Born into a Christian family, Faustus rose through the ecclesiastical ranks to become one of the most influential figures in the early Christian Church. His theological writings, although largely lost to history, had a lasting impact on the development of Western Christianity.

Faustus' opposition to Pelagianism, a theological movement that emphasized human free will and rejected the idea of original sin, helped shape the course of Christian theology for centuries to come. He was one of the first bishops to confront the Pelagians directly, using his influence to promote the orthodox view.

One of the most notable outcomes of Faustus' efforts was the Council of Carthage in 417 CE, which further solidified the rejection of Pelagianism and established a stronger emphasis on the role of God in human salvation. This event marked a significant turning point in the history of Western Christianity.

Despite his lasting impact, Faustus' life remains somewhat enshrouded in mystery. He died in 495 CE, leaving behind a legacy that continues to influence Christian theology and practice to this day.

Faustus' story serves as a testament to the enduring power of faith and conviction, even in the face of overwhelming opposition. His unwavering commitment to the orthodox view of original sin has left an indelible mark on the course of human history.
